borders.before: the lecturer's welcome, course context, and outline of learning objectives
borders.after: foundational definitions of cancer, mutation accumulation, microenvironment, and the roles of bad luck versus exposure
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 1 is framing and course introduction, while subtopic 2 begins substantive teaching on the biology of cancer development.
borders.caseForMoving: There is no other opening framing subtopic, so moving earlier or later would improperly mix introductory mechanics with content.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing it would merge introductory procedural remarks with core lecture content.

borders.before: epidemiological patterns and regional cancer incidence differences between genetics and environment
borders.after: specific infectious agents (H. pylori, EBV, HPV, retroviruses) and biological mechanisms driving cancer
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 6 concludes the high-level overview of etiology and geographic epidemiology, while subtopic 7 launches into granular molecular and biological mechanisms of specific agents.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 6 is clearly epidemiological framing; moving the border to 8 would strand the introduction of pathogens in the preceding section.
borders.caseForRemoving: The detailed survey of biological/chemical carcinogenic mechanisms (7-17) is a distinct major module from the conceptual framing of cancer risk factors and population variations (2-6).

borders.before: a summary of key mechanistic takeaways (mutagens, promoters, xenobiotics, age-specific factors)
borders.after: mutational signatures and high-throughput sequencing methods to detect carcinogen exposure
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 17 acts as a summary of the mechanistic section, and subtopic 18 shifts to methodologies and testing paradigms for identifying and proving carcinogenicity.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 17 summarizes prior content rather than introducing methodological testing tools, so 18 is the exact start of testing methods.
borders.caseForRemoving: Investigating how carcinogenicity is scientifically proven (signatures, epidemiology, animal models, Ames test) asks an entirely different question from how agents mutate or promote cells.

borders.before: the Ames test, in vitro assays, and toxicological screening limitations
borders.after: closing thoughts on risk versus benefit, final lecture takeaways, and concluding applause
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 22 delivers closing framing, synthesis of risk-benefit, and farewell/applause.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 21 is detailed content on the Ames test, so moving to 21 would bring technical testing details into the closing.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would conflate experimental toxicology assays with the lecture wrap-up.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 2 and 3 focus on intrinsic/bad-luck cellular biology, whereas 4-6 examine specific environmental exposures and geographical epidemiological studies.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 2 through 6 together build the overarching question of cancer etiology (bad luck, intrinsic mutation, genetics, and environment/epidemiology) before diving into specific biochemical mechanisms.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 7-13 focus primarily on direct and indirect mutagens (pathogens, chemical adducts, UV), while 14-17 focus on the two-stage model of promotion versus initiation and developmental timing.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 7-17 form a continuous mechanistic breakdown of the different classes of carcinogens (biological, dietary, chemical, promoters, tissue/developmental stage), concluding with a unified summary in 17.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 18-19 focus on human data (sequencing signatures, biobanks, epidemiology) whereas 20-21 cover experimental laboratory models (rodents, Ames test).
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 18 through 21 systematically answer the single methodological question of how carcinogenicity is proven across genomics, epidemiology, in vivo, and in vitro models.

topics.label: Lecture introduction and learning objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic provides the lecturer's welcome, course context, and outline of learning objectives.

topics.label: Cancer etiology: bad luck, genetics, and environmental exposure
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine the contributing factors to cancer development, balancing endogenous random mutations and genetic predispositions against environmental risks supported by epidemiological and population data.

topics.label: Mechanisms of chemical, physical, and biological carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics detail the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which infectious agents, chemical mutagens, radiation, and non-mutagenic promoters initiate and drive tumor formation.

topics.label: Methodologies for identifying and proving carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explore the experimental, genomic, and epidemiological tools used to demonstrate that specific agents cause cancer.

topics.label: Conclusion and risk-benefit analysis
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic concludes the lecture with overarching takeaways on lifestyle risks, regulatory challenges, and daily risk-benefit decisions.
